Thus, shading practices create temporary obstacles to the free movement of pedestrians, compounding other physical obstacles such as narrow sidewalks, poor pavement quality, holes, slopes, and other ob- stacles to circulation, such as urban furniture. These constraints vary according to certain times of the day and days of the week, as the cir- culation patterns and the informal retailers’ location and shading practices shift with the movement of the sun. Thus, people adjust their movement to mitigate thermal discomfort and stress, resulting in a dy- namic interaction between shading and urban rhythms. This phenomenon echoes the notion that thermalscapes, by shaping human movement across space, participate in the spatial choreographies of the city (Edensor & Hughes, 2021; Jensen et al., 2015). However, it also shows that thermalscapes can disrupt the flow of urban rhythms that are central to the vitality of urban consumption districts (Cachinho & Paiva, 2021; Ka¨rrholm, 2017). Not all interferences are perceived negatively; some participants reported feeling tranquil in these micro- spaces, appreciating the opportunities to browse products at a leisurely pace: We passed by one side; we were a bit squished. It had flip-flops on one side and the store on the other, but we still kept moving. (Participant 10). It was a calm walk, but the heat really bothered me. At a certain point, I was tired. (…) We passed by a part which was busier, where people were selling stuff. Exhibitors and stands. There, it was too much information. But it was cool because I like movement. (Participant 15). These findings not only reaffirm the fundamental role of thermal- scapes in shaping street rhythms (Abarghuie et al., 2022; Jensen & Fust´e-Forn´e, 2023), but also highlight the dimension of experience co- creation at play here, as participants respond differently to the rhythms created by the thermalscapes of Cuiab´a’s city centre. Taking into account that the success of shopping districts is often hinges on their ability to produce territories with vibrant rhythmic flows of consumers (Cachinho & Paiva, 2021; K¨arrholm, 2017; White et al., 2023), this insight underlines the dual necessity of recognising the impact of ther- malspaces on consumer experience and understanding the complex consumer responses to multi-sensory consumption-oriented atmo- Fig. 5. The synergy between formal and informal shading practices by Cuiab´a’s retailers very often compensates the inadequacy of the city’s public space for thermal mitigation (Eliasson et al., 2007; Elnabawi & Hamza, 2020a; Thorsson et al., 2004). Indeed, some participants mentioned that the lack of arborization of the streets was a problem because there was little natural shade. The shade provided by the buildings, the store awnings, and sun umbrellas was therefore valued by the participants, who always sought these shaded spaces throughout their walk. As participant 5 remarked: I walked always in the shade. There were moments here in the 13 de Junho Street in which it was fresher. It was cooler there, and there were fewer people. Shaded spaces are also valued for the possibility to stop and enjoy the wind that seldom blows through Cuiaba´’s city centre. Participants mentioned that the scarce moments in which the wind blew while they were in the shade were important moments to cool down and relax, which also underlines the interplay between local shading practices and the natural atmosphere. This underscores the importance of incorpo- rating such practices into urban planning to enhance the livability of hot city centres. JSON: Name: thermalscape_shade_biosensing Title: Ethnographic and participatory mobile-biosensing evaluation of the causal effect of informal shading practices on pedestrian thermal stress and consumption behaviour in hot urban centres Short Hypothesis: Informal shading (awnings, umbrellas/parasols, and shade under trees/balconies) causally reduces pedestrian electrodermal arousal and increases dwell time and purchase incidence in hot urban consumption streets compared to equivalent unshaded street segments. Related Work: Existing work on thermal comfort in urban contexts primarily follows two streams: quantitative microclimate and thermal-comfort modelling that estimate physiological comfort from environmental variables, and field studies that collect self-reported comfort or observational counts in selected sites. A smaller set of studies employ wearable physiological sensors but typically in controlled or semi-controlled settings and often report aggregate correlations between ambient measures and single-subject biosignals. Research on shading has emphasized formal, design-led interventions (tree planting, built shading, reflective surfaces) and their modeled thermal benefits, whereas informal shading practices (temporary awnings, vendor umbrellas, adaptive placement under balconies/trees) are sparsely documented. Key limitations in prior approaches are reliance on model-derived comfort metrics or self-report rather than in-situ physiological measures; limited integration of ethnographic, spatial and biosensor data; small, non-random samples; lack of causal designs or appropriate baselines; and scarce evidence linking thermal interventions directly to measurable consumption outcomes (dwell time, purchase incidence). Abstract: This research evaluates whether informal shading practices deployed in hot urban consumption streets causally reduce pedestrian thermal stress and influence consumption behaviour. We combine ethnographic mapping with a randomized participatory mobile-biosensing protocol: pedestrians complete pre-defined walking routes instrumented with wearable electrodermal activity (EDA), GPS, and simultaneous microclimate logging while encountering segments with different shading conditions (unshaded, awnings, vendor parasols, natural canopy). Post-walk elicitation interviews tie subjective experience to time-aligned physiological traces. The main contribution is an integrated methodological pipeline that produces causal estimates of shading type on physiological arousal, dwell time, walking speed, and purchase incidence, controlling for ambient temperature, humidity, pedestrian density, and participant effects. Expected outcomes include quantified effect sizes for common informal shading practices, spatial maps of high-value thermalscape territories, and validated metrics linking EDA changes to observable consumption behaviours. Results are intended to inform urban planning and retail management decisions for heat-resilient street-level consumption spaces. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Wearable biosensor dataset: continuous EDA (4 Hz or higher), heart rate, and accelerometer from Empatica E4 or equivalent for N=120 participants; (2) GPS traces and timestamped route segments; (3) Microclimate dataset: co-located air temperature, relative humidity, globe/solar irradiance, and wind speed sampled at 1-min resolution per route segment; (4) Behavioral logs: time-stamped dwell time at segment, walking speed, counts of stops, and transaction receipts/purchase incidence where available; (5) Elicitation interviews and short thermal comfort questionnaires (Likert scale) time-aligned to EDA events; (6) Geospatial layer: sidewalk width, awning/umbrella canopy footprint, tree canopy polygons and store footprints. Baselines: (A) Unshaded street segments (no awning/umbrella/canopy); (B) Formal fixed shading (permanent store awnings, pre-existing canopy); (C) Indoor air-conditioned baseline (entrance/exit proximal to AC stores). Experimental setup: Randomized within-subject route assignment where each participant traverses segments in randomized order to encounter each shading condition; sessions conducted across morning and late-afternoon time windows; microclimate sensors co-located at each segment; synchronized multimodal timestamping. Preprocessing: EDA signal filtering, tonic/phasic decomposition, artifact rejection based on accelerometer. Primary evaluation metrics: mean skin conductance level (SCL) per segment, phasic event count (SCRs per minute), mean walking speed, dwell time (seconds), purchase incidence (binary), subjective thermal comfort score. Statistical analysis: mixed-effects models with participant as random intercept, shading condition and microclimate variables as fixed effects; report coefficients, 95% CIs, and Cohen's d for contrasts. Comparison/ablation studies: (1) Shading-type ablation: contrast awning vs parasol vs tree canopy vs unshaded; (2) Data-modality ablation: model behavioural outcomes using (a) microclimate+context only, (b) microclimate+self-report, (c) microclimate+EDA, comparing predictive R^2 and AIC; (3) Temporal ablation: morning vs afternoon sessions. Power and sample plan: target N=120 with within-subject design to detect small-to-moderate effect (Cohen's d=0.35) with 80% power at alpha=0.05. Secondary analyses: time-series clustering of EDA events to identify micro-atmospheric episodes; spatial interpolation to produce thermalscape maps. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: wearable EDA sensors are prone to motion artifacts and sweat-baseline drift; poor sensor contact or device malfunction can produce unusable traces. Data/measurement biases: participant sample may be skewed toward volunteers comfortable with wearables, limiting representativeness; Hawthorne effects and altered behaviour due to being observed or interviewed. Confounders and causal inference limits: uncontrolled variables such as transient vehicle exhaust, store AC outflow, crowding, route microtopography, clothing level, hydration state, and individual acclimatization can confound shading effects despite mixed-model controls. Scalability constraints: logistics and cost of synchronized microclimate sensors and wearables limit multi-site and seasonal replication. Generalization limits: results derived from a single hot-city centre climate and cultural retail context may not extrapolate to temperate climates, differently regulated public spaces, or cities with different retail morphologies. Evaluation biases: EDA-based arousal is non-specific (responds to thermal, social, and emotional stimuli) and cannot uniquely attribute changes to thermal stress without triangulation. Ethical/privacy constraints: GPS and purchase logs raise privacy concerns that constrain available behavioural detail.
